source.title: Open Source Replication & Commentary on Anthropic's Dictionary Learning Paper

page_placements.theme: Interpretable features are not neuron-aligned: each spreads over many neurons

record.tranche_reason: The post trains a sparse autoencoder on a language-model MLP layer and measures its latent features and their relation to the neuron basis. This bears conceptually on whether more sparse features than neurons can be represented, but it does not directly measure individual neurons’ responses to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The results concern sparse-autoencoder features, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. They bear on V3 through the number, interpretability, and decoder-weight distribution of extracted features; they do not establish that neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition.
record.test_reason: The post replicates sparse-autoencoder dictionary learning on the gelu-1l MLP layer. It takes superposition as the working assumption and reports the SAE's own outputs: feature interpretability, decoder density in the neuron basis, the ultra-low-frequency cluster and reconstruction loss. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how many neurons are polysemantic, or what causes polysemanticity. The findings concern SAE latents, a related but different construct, so they go under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The author says the core SAE results replicate, with a significant fraction of features interpretable. He also says features are mostly dense in the neuron basis, which he finds surprising, though kurtosis shows the neuron basis is still privileged. He reports an ultra-low-frequency cluster (about 60% of features) whose encoder weights share one direction. That direction recurs across random seeds, and he could not interpret it.
record.recipe_differences: Replicates the sparse-autoencoder approach on the MLP layer of an open-source one-layer GELU language model, with implementation differences including neuron resampling, training-buffer construction, and a decoder-norm bug.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that the ultra-low-frequency cluster differed from the referenced A/1 autoencoder and speculates that resampling choices may explain the discrepancy. It also reports that a different random seed yielded a similar shared encoder direction, while an orthogonality constraint produced a cluster in a different direction.

fits_no_version.finding: For non-ultra-low-frequency SAE features on the gelu-1l MLP, about 92.1% of decoder vectors are dense in the neuron basis, about 3.9% are 1-sparse and about 4.0% are 10-ish-sparse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary features extracted from language-model MLP layers are mostly distributed across many neurons rather than aligned with single neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder-weight kurtosis is well above a random Gaussian baseline for almost all features, so the neuron basis is still privileged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Even neuron-dense SAE features show a privileged neuron basis.

fits_no_version.finding: Anecdotally, 6 of the first 8 non-ultra-low-frequency SAE features seemed interpretable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features on a 1L language-model MLP layer are often interpretable.

record.problems: The author says the interpretability check was anecdotal and not rigorous. The author reports failing to properly fix the decoder norm to 1, which may have affected other results. The ultra-low-frequency cluster is not interpreted, and the feature-count result does not establish that the latents are distinct natural features or that neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported outcomes were included because they concern ultra-low-frequency feature behavior, autoencoder optimization or geometry, or reconstruction performance rather than the claim versions tested here.

untested.parts: No share or rate of polysemantic MLP neurons is measured.
No direct test that neurons are polysemantic because more sparse features are packed into fewer neurons; SAE latents are not shown to be the model's true features.

record.verdict_notes: This is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed replication blog post. It contains a known bug: the decoder norm was not properly fixed to 1, which may have affected other results. The reader's V3 'supports' label is removed: the study does not test neuron polysemanticity or its cause.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test vision models or image-classifier neurons.
Does not measure the share of polysemantic MLP neurons or their responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.

Does not directly measure neuron polysemanticity or establish that superposition causes it; the extracted features are sparse-autoencoder latents, and the post notes that many ultra-low-frequency latents may be problematic.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of neuron polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.
Does not compare polysemantic-neuron shares across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings, nor assess performance costs of reducing that share.
Does not investigate whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or whether unrelated neuron mixtures are rare.
Does not compare measurements or explanation-scoring choices for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

rows.operation_detail: Reports the number of sparse-autoencoder features trained on the MLP layer relative to its neuron count.
rows.measure: SAE feature count compared with MLP neuron count
rows.note: The feature count exceeds the neuron count, but the post does not establish that each latent is a distinct underlying model feature or that this causes polysemantic neuron responses.
rows.check: 16384 is the SAE width the author chose, not a result. It is a design value and should not be a result row; it says nothing about how many features the model represents.

rows.operation_detail: Measures how much of each SAE decoder vector’s squared weight mass is explained by the largest neuron weights.
rows.measure: Fraction of features classified by decoder-weight concentration
rows.note: The post defines dense features as fve_top_10<0.35, 1-sparse as fve_top_1>0.35 and fve_next_9<0.1, and describes the remaining group as 10-ish-sparse. These are decoder-weight distributions in the neuron basis, not a measure of sparse feature activity.
rows.check: This measures how SAE decoder weights spread across neurons, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. It is consistent with features not being neuron-aligned but does not show superposition causes neuron polysemanticity. Belongs in fits_no_version.

relation.reason: Superposition and polysemanticity are the motivating premise for training the SAE ('extract interpretable features from superposition'). No result tests whether neurons are polysemantic.

tranche.reason: The post replicates SAE dictionary learning, which is premised on superposition. It reports only the SAE's own outputs: interpretability of features, decoder density, the ultra-low-frequency cluster and reconstruction loss. It never measures whether gelu-1l neurons respond to unrelated inputs and never compares neurons with features for interpretability, so it is not T2 on the polysemanticity question.

source_check.notes: R2 describes how SAE decoder weights spread over the 2048 neurons, not whether neurons are polysemantic. Kurtosis still shows the neuron basis is privileged. The author reports a bug: decoder norms were not reset to 1, which 'may have affected my other results'. Neel Nanda shares authorship with an original.

statements.problem: None. The text gives ~92.1% dense (fve_top_10<0.35), ~3.9% 1-sparse and ~4.0% 10-ish-sparse for non-ultra-low-frequency features. These come from decoder weights in the gelu-1l MLP neuron basis.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAE features extracted from the gelu-1l MLP layer
reader_labels.reason: The SAE produced 16384 features from a layer with 2048 neurons, most measured decoder vectors were dense in the neuron basis, and 6 of 8 inspected features seemed interpretable (R1–R3). This supports the feasibility of a feature decomposition with more latents than neurons, not the causal claim about neuron polysemanticity itself.
